routes.description: Establish that contingent existence, religious experience, or moral obligation provides a defensible inference to an objective transcendent ground identifiable with God.
routes.successCriteria: At least one affirmative line must connect the relevant experience or fact to a necessary, objective, and non-arbitrary divine ground while answering the principal non-theistic alternative.

motionBridge.description: Show that at least one of the three proposed domains warrants affirming God's existence rather than merely describing human thought or feeling.

centralBridges.description: Connect experienced contingent beings and their totality to an external sufficient reason that does not itself require a further explanation.
Show that the character of religious experience is better explained by an objective transcendent cause than by a wholly subjective account.
Connect objective moral obligation and the authority of moral law to a transcendent ground of value that is neither arbitrary nor socially contingent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish an experiential inference to a necessary being from an a priori attempt to define that being into existence.
Explain how moral disagreement and culturally variable precepts remain open to criticism by reference to an objective ideal order.

routes.description: Show that the contingency, religious-experience, and moral-obligation arguments do not require God because their key inferences are invalid, underdetermined, or matched by non-theistic explanations.
routes.successCriteria: Prevent each affirmative line from reaching its divine conclusion by challenging its central inference or supplying an adequate account that does not presuppose a transcendent being.

motionBridge.description: Show that none of the proposed domains supplies sufficient grounds for moving from observed experience or practice to God's existence.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the application of necessity to beings and the inference from explanations of particular contingent things to an explanation of their totality.
Show that private experiences and their beneficial effects cannot discriminate an external divine object from subjective or incompatible interpretations.
Account for moral discrimination and obligation through feeling, custom, education, or imagined social disapproval without invoking divine authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require that claims about a being whose essence includes existence avoid treating existence as a predicate or reviving an ontological inference.
Use historical and cultural variation in perceived duties to test the asserted universality and absoluteness of moral law.

sections.title: Contingency and the meaning of necessary existence
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an empirically encountered contingent being can support a coherent modal inference to a being that cannot fail to exist.

sections.title: The totality of contingent beings and sufficient reason
sections.rationale: This issue tests the indispensable move from explanations within the world to an external explanation of the world or totality as such.

sections.title: Religious experience and an objective transcendent cause
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the distinctive character of mystical awareness supplies grounds for an objective divine reality rather than a subjective event.

sections.title: Competing reports and transformative effects
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether conviction, beneficial transformation, and experiential veracity can distinguish divine contact from incompatible or fictional objects.

sections.title: Moral feeling, objective value, and critical standards
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether moral distinctions require an objective standard and whether identifying goodness with a divine source establishes rather than assumes God.

sections.title: Moral obligation, variation, and its explanatory ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the authoritative sense of obligation requires a transcendent lawgiver or is adequately explained by historical customs, education, and social disapproval.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Because no contingent object contains the reason for its own existence, the totality of contingent objects requires a sufficient reason external to that totality.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is Copleston's announced, uninterrupted statement of his metaphysical argument from contingency.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly supplies the contingency route's proposed bridge from contingent objects to an external sufficient reason for their totality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops the indispensable explanatory bridge for its selected route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but the relation between each contingent object and the totality is not fully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is asserted as required although the transfer of sufficient reason from members to totality remains undefended.

charity.alternative: The totality is only the collection of its contingent members, not an additional object.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even on that reading, applying the explanatory demand distributively does not yet establish one external reason for the collection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is orderly but leaves a material bridge from unexplained members to an externally explained totality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It relies on the asserted universal sufficient-reason principle without defending its scope or comparing a brute-totality alternative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the indispensable external-sufficient-reason bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes that the world is not an extra object, but compresses the decisive distributive-to-collective bridge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says no experienced object contains its own reason and concludes that the totality must have an external existent reason.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions, so a necessary being is admissible only if denying that being's existence is self-contradictory.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell explicitly introduces this as his starting answer to Copleston's argument and develops it in one turn.

components.text: The proposed external reason must be a coherent necessary being rather than another unexplained existent.

response.rationale: Russell directly challenges the modal status required of the external reason by restricting meaningful necessity to analytic propositions, though he does not address the totality inference itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive necessary-being component while leaving the totality-demand component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criterion for necessity and the condition for admitting a necessary being are expressly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The restriction of necessity to analytic propositions is firm and clear, but its exclusivity receives little defense in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Necessary existence may be a metaphysical status inferred from contingent reality rather than an analytic existence proposition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell's semantic restriction needs an argument showing that this modal use is illegitimate rather than merely nonanalytic.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional challenge is internally coherent, but the exclusive restriction of necessity to analytic propositions is a material unsupported premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The semantic thesis is asserted without representative analysis of rival metaphysical uses of necessity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it strongly attacks a necessary component of the contingency route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response targets the strongest modal claim but largely stipulates a narrower conception of necessity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell states that necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions and would admit a necessary being only if its nonexistence were contradictory.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Although the existence of a contingent being must be learned from experience, once such a being is known to exist, the inference to a necessary being follows with necessity.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston states the conditional proposition, accepts Russell's terminology provisionally, and distinguishes its empirical premise.

components.text: A necessary conclusion may be conditional on an empirically discovered contingent being rather than resting on an analytic existential premise.

response.rationale: Copleston directly distinguishes the empirical antecedent from the claimed necessary consequence, answering Russell's assimilation of the argument to a wholly analytic proof.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the decisive analytic-versus-empirical objection, though it does not demonstrate the claimed entailment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The empirical antecedent and allegedly necessary conditional consequence are clearly separated and qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional structure is explicit, but the excerpt asserts rather than proves that contingency entails a necessary being.

charity.alternative: Russell can grant an empirical antecedent while denying that it analytically or metaphysically entails a necessary being.
charity.decisiveQualification: Distinguishing the premise's epistemic source does not itself establish the modal entailment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction is coherent, but the central conditional from a contingent existent to a necessary being remains a material unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No supporting modal demonstration is supplied for the claimed necessary consequence of the empirical premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supports the distinction between experiential inference and a priori definition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly narrows Russell's objection but leaves the strongest residual challenge to the inference unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that a contingent being is discovered through experience while claiming that, once known, a necessary being follows.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Defining a being whose essence involves existence revives the ontological argument, but existence is not a predicate and cannot be asserted analytically of a named subject.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell identifies the alleged ontological implication and then gives his logical account of meaningful existence claims.

components.text: The asserted necessary being appears to require treating its existence as analytically included in its essence.
The external sufficient reason must be characterized without illegitimately making existence a predicate of a named being.

response.rationale: Russell identifies the alleged slide into an ontological argument, explains that existence is not a predicate, and states the consequence that analytic existence cannot be asserted of a named subject.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the inferential failure and states why the proposed analytic existence claim is unavailable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The target, logical distinction between names and descriptions, and predicate objection are all recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical objection is clearly framed, though its application to every experiential necessary-being inference is broader than demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Copleston may infer a being and only subsequently infer essence-existence identity, rather than define it into existence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell's predicate objection defeats an analytic existence proof but does not alone defeat that posterior identity inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The logical analysis is consistent and diagnostic, with a bounded gap in showing that Copleston's inference actually commits the targeted error.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The name-description and predicate analysis supports the objection, though rival accounts of existential quantification are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it very directly advances the existence-analysis requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection handles the ontological reading strongly but only partly accommodates the experiential reading.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell calls the position an ontological argument, denies that named subjects can significantly be said to exist, and says existence is not a predicate.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: God is inferred from experience rather than known a priori, and divine essence and existence must be identical because otherwise God's existence would require a sufficient reason beyond God.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston expressly distinguishes his experiential inference from an argument based solely on an intuition of God's essence.

components.text: God's existence is inferred from experience before essence-existence identity is argued, so existence is not inserted into an a priori definition.
Knowledge of the relevant being begins from experience rather than an analytic existential proposition.

response.rationale: Copleston directly rejects the a priori ontological reading and offers a sufficient-reason argument for subsequent essence-existence identity, although that new inference remains compressed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply fully contacts the predicate and analytic-proof objections, with one important bridge in its positive replacement argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The temporal and inferential ordering of experiential knowledge and later identity reasoning is clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction from a priori proof is well matched, but the identity conclusion is stronger than the abbreviated sufficient-reason warrant.

charity.alternative: Even a posterior inference may still misuse existence when it concludes that essence and existence are identical.
charity.decisiveQualification: Avoiding an a priori definition answers one objection but does not by itself establish the coherence or truth of the identity claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The sequence is coherent, but the move from no reason beyond God to essence-existence identity leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The experiential starting point is explicit, while the sufficient-reason warrant for identity is only briefly asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it almost maximally supports separation from an a priori existence proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately handles the strongest ontological reading while leaving the residual logical question open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston says God's essence is not known a priori, that existence is inferred through world experience, and that nonidentity would require a reason beyond God.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Although observation supports causal explanations for particular things, it supplies no reason to suppose that the totality of particular things has any cause whatsoever.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell grants causal explanation for a particular object and immediately rejects extending that concept to the totality.

components.text: Explanatory practices concerning particular objects do not by themselves license a causal or sufficient-reason demand for their totality.

response.rationale: Russell expressly identifies the part-to-whole extension as unsupported and states the defeating consequence that there is no supplied reason to posit a cause of all particular objects.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response explicitly attacks the decisive totality inference and gives the consequence for the proposed external explanation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge is clear, though cause and explanation are used with only a brief indication of their relation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Russell claims only that no reason has been supplied for the totality extension, a force matched by his diagnostic point.

charity.alternative: The demand concerns a sufficient reason for contingent existence, not necessarily an observed temporal cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell's causal formulation does not fully address a broader noncausal principle of sufficient reason.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The refusal to transfer an observed explanatory concept to the totality is coherent, with a bounded cause-versus-reason ambiguity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The distinction between particular observations and totality is directly supported, but the broader sufficient-reason alternative is not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the indispensable totality-explanation inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply strongly challenges the observed-causation route but partly narrows the opponent's explanatory demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell grants causal explanation for particular objects but says observation supplies no reason whatsoever to suppose the totality has a cause.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The basic mystical awareness of a loving, transcendent, nonconceptual reality is more adequately explained by an objective cause than as an experience produced wholly within the subject.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston announces the religious-experience topic, defines the relevant experience, and states his explanatory inference.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances the religious-experience route by describing the purportedly transcendent phenomenology and preferring an objective cause over a wholly subjective explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the route's central objective-cause inference but compresses alternative comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The type of experience, subjective alternative, and comparative explanatory conclusion are expressly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Claiming inadequate subjective explanation is stronger than the phenomenological description alone warrants without rival testing.

charity.alternative: A wholly subjective event can phenomenologically present itself as indubitable, loving, and self-transcending.
charity.decisiveQualification: The felt character of externality does not independently discriminate an external cause from subjective production.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory form is coherent, but the bridge from seeming transcendence to an objective transcendent cause remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant rests substantially on phenomenological description without independent verification or serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports the objective-cause bridge for religious experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the subjective account but does not develop its strongest capacity to mimic the cited phenomenology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes an indubitable-seeming transcendent awareness and claims that its basic character cannot be adequately explained wholly subjectively.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Private mystical reports do not establish God because equally convinced reports concern demons or Satan, which cannot all be accepted on the same testimonial basis.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell states his agnostic conclusion and compares mystical testimony with similarly confident reports of rejected supernatural beings.

components.text: The same private experiential confidence supports incompatible supernatural objects, so testimonial phenomenology does not discriminate God.

response.rationale: Russell identifies the parity problem, supplies Satan and demon reports as incompatible comparators, and concludes that the same testimonial basis cannot establish God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly diagnoses the decisive discrimination failure and states its consequence for the God inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential basis, comparator class, incompatibility, and skeptical consequence are all clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is limited to what can be inferred from reports, matching the force of the parity counterexample.

charity.alternative: Theistic mystical reports might possess distinctive content or fruits absent from demonic reports.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell's parity holds only absent an independently defended discriminator among the report types.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The incompatible-report parity argument is explicit and consistent, with only a bounded assumption of relevant experiential similarity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete comparator reports support underdetermination, though representativeness and detailed phenomenological equivalence are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the route's required objective-cause discrimination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly targets undifferentiated testimonial reliance while leaving room for a discriminator not supplied in the target move.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell compares mystical reports of God with equally confident purely mental reports of Satan and denies that the former uniquely support God.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: A profound and wholesome transformation caused by an experience is not evidence that the experience involved any reality outside the subject.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell appeals to his own transformative experiences and explicitly denies that their effects evidence an external object.

components.text: Wholesome transformation caused by an experience does not verify that the experience has an object outside the subject.

response.rationale: Russell separates beneficial effects from external-object verification and uses his own transformative experiences to state the defeating evidential consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply clearly diagnoses why a proposed corroborating effect cannot establish the target's external-cause conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between transformative effect and evidence of an external object is clear and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force is appropriately limited to denying that beneficial effects by themselves verify external reality.

charity.alternative: Transformation may be corroborative evidence when combined with distinctive phenomenology rather than a standalone proof.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell defeats transformation as sufficient verification but does not show it has no incremental evidential relevance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The separation of causal personal effect from truth about an external object is explicit, consistent, and inferentially strong.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The personal counterexample illustrates the logical independence well, though it is anecdotal rather than representative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it materially attacks corroboration for the religious-experience bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response handles the standalone argument fairly while leaving the cumulative-evidence possibility open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell cites profound wholesome changes in his own character while denying that these changes evidenced anything existing outside him.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: A morally beneficial response to a loved historical or fictional figure does not establish that the figure actually exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly develops Russell's skeptical counterexample and is followed by Copleston's explicit agreement and qualification.

components.text: Beneficial influence from a loved figure does not establish that the figure exists, because fictional figures can produce the same effect.

response.rationale: Russell supplies a counterexample to the inference from beneficial influence to existence and states the consequence that an affecting object need not be an existing one.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The counterexample expressly defeats the existence inference, though it addresses effects more directly than mystical phenomenology.

precisionFindings.rationale: The fictional comparator and the limited conclusion about beneficial influence are clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As a counterexample to sufficiency, one coherent fictional case warrants the asserted defeating conclusion.

charity.alternative: Direct mystical acquaintance purports to be present awareness, unlike influence mediated by a narrative about a figure.
charity.decisiveQualification: The counterexample defeats beneficial effect as verification but not every inference based on alleged direct acquaintance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample validly rebuts beneficial influence as a sufficient condition for the influencing figure's existence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The fictional-figure example is apt for the limited sufficiency claim, with a bounded analogy gap regarding direct experience.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it materially attacks a corroborating path to objective religious reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response is fair to the effects argument but its analogy is incomplete for the target's distinctive experiential claim.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell describes a person morally improved by devotion to a fictional figure and notes that the effect does not make the figure existent.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Identifying love of genuine goodness with love of God risks merely defining God as goodness rather than independently establishing God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell frames the position as a direct question to Copleston, whose immediately following answer accepts that further argument is required.

components.text: The objective-cause inference from mystical phenomenology requires independent discrimination from subjective explanations.

response.rationale: Russell raises a relevant theological circularity question about defining God as goodness, but it does not contact the earlier mystical-experience move's decisive objective-cause demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, the question bears on establishing God but does not answer the selected target's experiential inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The question clearly distinguishes defining God through goodness from independently arguing for God's existence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interrogative and conditional framing accurately match the limited diagnostic basis supplied in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Goodness may reflect God without being identical to God, given an independently established theology.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell correctly notes that this interpretation cannot itself provide that independent establishment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional circularity diagnosis is explicit, consistent, and properly limited to the proposed identification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The wording of the proposed identification itself supports the diagnostic question, with independent premises expressly left open.

relevanceBurden.rationale: No exact locked burden is contacted because the legal target is the earlier mystical-experience move rather than the later moral exchange.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question openly allows that further argument could avoid the circularity and identifies exactly what is needed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell asks whether God is being defined as the system of goodness and says that, if so, the claim requires further argument.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Goodness is not identical with God in a pantheistic sense, but what is truly good reflects and proceeds from God, though this interpretation depends on independently recognizing God's existence.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer explicitly rejects pantheism, states Copleston's own theological view, and concedes the dependence of that interpretation on God's existence.

components.text: Goodness is not simply identical with God; it reflects and proceeds from God, and that interpretation depends on independently recognizing God.

response.rationale: Copleston directly rejects the pantheistic definition and concedes the need for independent recognition of God, fully contacting Russell's circularity concern without establishing that independent premise here.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly answers both the identity question and the decisive independence qualification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rejection of identity, reflection relation, and dependence on prior recognition are all expressly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The theological interpretation is carefully qualified as dependent on an independently established divine existence.

charity.alternative: Russell's concern is not limited to pantheism but includes any use of goodness to establish the God from whom goodness allegedly proceeds.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston concedes that the interpretation depends on prior recognition and therefore does not use it as an independent proof here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinctions are explicit and internally consistent, and the concession prevents the statement from functioning circularly as a proof.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conditional theological interpretation is coherent, but no evidence is offered here for the claimed procession of goodness from God.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply resolves a local objection but does not itself contact an exact locked route bridge strongly enough.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately addresses the stronger circularity concern and preserves its decisive qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston denies pantheistic identity, says goodness reflects and proceeds from God, and expressly concedes dependence on recognizing God's existence.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Moral distinctions need no external theological justification because good and bad can be discriminated through feeling, much as colors are distinguished through perception.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell answers Copleston's direct question in the first person and sustains the perceptual analogy until Copleston introduces a concrete moral test case.

components.text: The claim that genuine goodness reflects and proceeds from God requires support beyond prior recognition of God.

response.rationale: Russell supplies an issue-bearing naturalistic account of moral discrimination through feeling, but it does not answer the selected target's conditional reflection-and-source claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it advances an alternative moral epistemology without contacting the target's decisive conditional claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The feeling analogy is recoverable, but feeling shifts between a discriminating faculty and the apparent basis of moral status.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy makes the account plausible, but it does not fully justify the broader claim that no external standard is required.

charity.alternative: Feeling may disclose objective moral properties rather than constitute or exhaust their authority.
charity.decisiveQualification: The color analogy supports discrimination through feeling but does not settle the ontology or normativity of what is discriminated.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The perceptual analogy is intelligible but leaves a material ambiguity between moral epistemology and moral ontology.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The position relies on analogy and assertion without showing that feeling adequately explains correctness or obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports a non-theological account of moral discrimination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The analogy compresses the strongest realist interpretation and leaves its decisive qualification unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell says good and bad are distinguished by feeling as blue and yellow are distinguished by seeing.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Differences in felt response cannot by themselves settle whether a judgment is sound, because without an objective criterion beyond feeling there is no basis for condemning even atrocious conduct.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn continues Copleston's questioning of Russell's feeling theory and contrasts the commandant's behavior with exemplary religious conduct.

components.text: Feeling alone cannot supply a correctness standard when agents feel differently about conduct, including atrocious conduct.

response.rationale: Copleston tests the feeling account with disagreement and atrocity, identifies the absence of an objective criterion, and states the consequence that condemnation lacks a basis on feeling alone.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly attacks the decisive adequacy of feeling as a moral standard and states the skeptical consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The target, disagreement test, objective-criterion demand, and condemnation consequence are all clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The need for some correctness criterion is well supported, but the move does not yet show that the criterion must be transcendent.

charity.alternative: A feeling-based theory can appeal to normal human capacities, informed reflection, or intersubjective correction rather than raw individual response.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those resources require articulation and may still fail to yield an objective standard independent of attitudes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The disagreement and atrocity test coherently exposes a missing norm of correctness in the simple feeling account.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The concrete counterexample strongly tests individual feeling, though broader naturalistic standards are not seriously compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it strongly attacks the adequacy of the non-theological moral account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection allows the normal-capacity response in the exchange but does not fully explore its strongest form.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston asks how conduct can be condemned when responses differ and argues that feeling alone supplies no objective criterion.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The perception of values and consciousness of moral obligation are best explained by a transcendent ground of value and a non-arbitrary author of moral law.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston explicitly introduces moral obligation as an approach to God's existence and states the explanatory hypothesis in an uninterrupted turn.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly presents the moral-obligation route by treating perceived value and felt obligation as best explained by a transcendent, non-arbitrary source.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly advances the indispensable moral-ground bridge while leaving alternative comparison compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explananda, comparative hypothesis, transcendent ground, and non-arbitrariness qualification are clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The best-explanation claim exceeds the support supplied because naturalistic accounts are not examined in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Moral perception and obligation may arise from rational, social, emotional, or evolutionary sources without a transcendent author.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must compare those alternatives and explain why authority specifically requires a personal divine source.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is coherent, but the bridge from authoritative obligation to a transcendent author is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts comparative superiority without representative support or serious assessment of non-theistic explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports the indispensable transcendent-ground-of-obligation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The non-arbitrariness qualification is useful, but the strongest non-theistic explanatory family is largely omitted.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston says perception of values and moral obligation are best explained by a transcendent ground and non-arbitrary author of moral law.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: There is no absolute moral law because perceived moral requirements change historically, with practices such as cannibalism once regarded as duties.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell explicitly rejects absoluteness and immediately supplies historical moral variation as his supporting example before Copleston answers.

components.text: Historically changing perceptions of duty challenge the asserted absoluteness and universal recognition of moral law.

response.rationale: Russell directly challenges absoluteness with historical variation and a cannibalism example, but this contacts recognition and content more than the claimed ground of obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts a material universality component while leaving the transcendent-ground inference largely unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The variation claim is clear, but movement in perceived duties is generalized into denial of any absolute moral law.

calibrationFindings.rationale: One historical example supports variation in accepted duties but not the categorical denial of every absolute moral standard.

charity.alternative: Changing moral beliefs can reflect error or development relative to an unchanged objective standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: Variation undermines universality of recognition but does not by itself disprove objective or absolute truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from historical disagreement to no absolute law contains a substantial truth-versus-belief gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cannibalism illustrates variation but is selective and insufficient for the universal conclusion asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supplies the historical-variation test specified by the route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially compresses the error-theory response and omits its decisive truth-versus-belief qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Russell denies anything absolute, says moral law changes, and cites a period when cannibalism was widely regarded as a duty.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The possibility of criticizing culturally accepted moral codes presupposes an objective ideal moral order whose obligatory character can be recognized and whose real foundation is God.
moves.attributionBasis: Copleston rejects divine dictation of particular precepts, distinguishes their variable content from an objective standard, and concludes with God as foundation.

components.text: The possibility of criticizing accepted codes distinguishes variable moral beliefs from an objective ideal standard.
An objective ideal order supplies a correctness standard beyond the feelings or conventions of a group.

response.rationale: Copleston directly answers variation by distinguishing accepted codes from an ideal critical standard, then links that standard to God, though the final foundation inference remains compressed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply fully contacts the variation challenge and also addresses the earlier feeling account's missing critical standard.

precisionFindings.rationale: The accepted-code versus ideal-order distinction is clear, while the mode of the order's imposition is only implicitly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Criticism supports a norm beyond current acceptance, but the claim that its real foundation is God is insufficiently warranted.

charity.alternative: Criticism of a code may use immanent consistency, human interests, or revisable rational standards without a transcendent ideal order.
charity.decisiveQualification: The mere practice of criticism does not decide among objective, constructivist, and immanent standards.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between codes and a critical standard is coherent, but the move from such a standard to God is a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The possibility of criticism supports some evaluative norm but does not independently support an ideal order founded in God.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it maximally supports objective criticism across variable moral codes.

moves.evidenceBasis: Copleston says criticism of accepted codes presupposes an objective ideal moral order and concludes that its real foundation is God.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: The sense of moral obligation can be explained as imagined disapproval produced by customs, taboos, environment, and education rather than by a transcendent lawgiver.
moves.attributionBasis: Russell states a first-person explanatory account of the sense of ought, after which Copleston explicitly answers by distinguishing moral form from content.

components.text: The experienced sense of ought can be explained through imagined disapproval, custom, taboo, environment, and education rather than God.
A naturalistic causal account is offered for moral obligation, opposing the claim that a transcendent lawgiver best explains it.

response.rationale: Russell directly supplies a non-theistic explanation of obligation and thereby contacts the divine-foundation claim, although the account does not fully explain objective correctness or categorical authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the explanatory demand with a rival account but leaves important normative components unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal proposal is clear, but imagined disapproval, customs, and education are not fully integrated into one stable mechanism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Russell presents the account as his view, but its claim to explain what ought means is stronger than the brief causal sketch warrants.

charity.alternative: Social formation may explain why obligation is felt without explaining whether obligations are valid or categorically authoritative.
charity.decisiveQualification: A causal genealogy of the feeling is not yet a normative account of objective obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The naturalistic mechanism is intelligible, but it risks conflating the origin of an ought-feeling with the meaning and authority of ought.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Custom, taboo, environment, and education are plausible mechanisms, but the excerpt offers no representative support or alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the route's non-theological account of moral obligation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the psychological explanandum but materially compresses the opponent's strongest authority and validity demand.
